conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You were brought in from rehab because of confusion and worsening hallucinations. Can you tell me how you’re feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a little better. The voices and shadows are still there, but not as bad. I was so scared last night. They said my pain meds might be part of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we think the oxycodone and Flexeril may have made your confusion worse. We’ve stopped both. You’re also on risperidone for hallucinations, which helps, but we’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know those could affect my mind. I just took them for back pain. Is that why I couldn’t think straight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. We also found signs of a urinary tract infection. That can worsen confusion, especially with your liver condition. We’ve started antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t feel like I had a UTI. No burning or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common, especially in older adults or those with chronic illness. Symptoms aren’t always typical. Your urine test showed infection, so we’re treating it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My stomach and back still hurt. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re avoiding opioids now. They can worsen confusion and constipation. We’ve started a new medication called lubiprostone for your bowel movements, and you can take Tylenol for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this pain for years. Is it from my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver is enlarged, which can cause discomfort. But your pain seems more related to chronic constipation. The lubiprostone should help. We’ll see if your pain improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my face? It drooped last time, and sometimes I can’t feel the left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your last admission. The MRI and CT showed no stroke. Your symptoms come and go, even when you’re asleep they’re gone. Neurology thinks it’s not a nerve problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is it? It feels real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may be related to stress or your overall health. Your liver disease affects your brain function. We call that hepatic encephalopathy. It can cause odd symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my liver is making me confused and my face droop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. This time, we think the infection and meds made it worse. We’re treating the UTI and keeping you off sedating drugs. Your mental clarity has already improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your kidney function was a bit low when you came in—creatinine up to 1.2. But after fluids, it’s back to 1.0. That’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my kidney damaged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it was just dehydration. Your liver disease makes you sensitive to fluid changes. We’ll keep encouraging you to drink and eat well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My white blood cell count is high. Is that infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was 13.6, which is high, but it’s likely from the UTI and also from not eating much. When you’re dehydrated, counts concentrate. We’ll repeat it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the chest X-ray? I saw something about a spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did see a shadow, but a second X-ray showed it’s gone. Likely just overlapping tissue. No pneumonia or lung issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. diff test came back negative, so we don’t need to treat for that. Your urine culture grew mixed bacteria, but since you’ve had VRE before, we’re sticking with ampicillin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I still need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for one more week. Even though the culture was mixed, we’re finishing the course because of your history. It’s oral, so you can take it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the lubiprostone—is that working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ve had regular bowel movements and your pain is better. We’re glad we could avoid opioids. They can make constipation and confusion worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs today show your ammonia level is normal, and you’re alert and oriented. That’s a big improvement from when you came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel more like myself. But sometimes my face still feels numb on the left.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noted that. It comes and goes, and there’s no nerve damage on imaging. It may be related to how your brain processes sensation, especially under stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I see a psychiatrist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not recommending that now. But if symptoms worsen, your primary doctor can help decide if a referral is needed. For now, we focus on your liver and overall health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’ll finish the ampicillin, keep taking lactulose and rifaximin for your liver, and stay on the lubiprostone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m going back to rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to extended care. They’ll help with your daily needs. We’re also sending reminders to avoid opioids and benzodiazepines—they can trigger confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the mass on my spine? The MRI mentioned it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a small benign tumor, likely a schwannoma. It hasn’t changed in size. You’ll need a yearly MRI to monitor it, but it’s not causing symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my transplant evaluation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s still ongoing. Your MELD score is stable. Continue with your liver team for follow-up. Avoid alcohol completely—it’s crucial for your candidacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a drink in months. I want this chance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Your commitment matters. We’ll keep supporting you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go. Your mental status is clear, infection is treated, and pain is controlled without opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What signs should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you become confused again, have fever, or your face droops and doesn’t improve, come back. Also, finish all your antibiotics and keep your follow-up labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no pain pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use Tylenol and tramadol only if absolutely needed. Avoid oxycodone. It’s safer for your liver and brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best. Thank you for helping me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
